subsystems.name: Qubit chip
subsystems.role: the processor itself: a lattice of superconducting loops whose circulating currents represent problem variables, with couplers between them.

subsystems.name: Cryogenic system
subsystems.role: keeps the chip at millikelvin temperatures so the circuits are superconducting and thermal noise is negligible.

subsystems.name: Magnetic shielding
subsystems.role: blocks Earth's field and external interference that would corrupt the qubits.

subsystems.name: Control and readout electronics
subsystems.role: sets the initial transverse field, the problem biases and couplers, then reads out each qubit's final state.

subsystems.name: Software stack
subsystems.role: turns a user's optimisation problem into a schedule of magnetic fields the hardware can run.
parts: problem mapping to quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation (QUBO)
minor embedding onto the chip's connectivity graph

buildSteps.title: Define the qubit topology
buildSteps.detail: Designers choose the layout of qubits and couplers — for example a chimera or pegasus graph — which sets how many variables a problem can hold and how easily it embeds.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the chip
buildSteps.detail: Niobium and aluminium films are deposited on a silicon wafer and patterned by lithography; Josephson junctions are formed by oxidising a thin aluminium layer between two electrodes.

buildSteps.title: Package and wire-bond
buildSteps.detail: The chip is mounted in a superconducting package and connected to control lines that carry magnetic flux to each qubit and coupler.

buildSteps.title: Cool and shield
buildSteps.detail: The package is loaded into a dilution refrigerator, cooled to around 10–20 millikelvin, and enclosed in magnetic shielding.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the qubits
buildSteps.detail: Each qubit's persistent current, inductance and coupler strength are measured and tuned so that the intended problem Hamiltonian can be realised.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the anneal
buildSteps.detail: Engineers run the transverse field down over a chosen time and map how often the system lands in the lowest-energy state, adjusting schedules to reduce errors.

buildSteps.title: Embed and run problems
buildSteps.detail: A user's problem is mapped to the chip's graph, embedded in software, then submitted; the chip anneals once per sample and returns many readouts.

buildSteps.title: Interpret results
buildSteps.detail: Readouts are corrected for bias and returned as candidate solutions; classical software then checks and refines them.

prerequisites.why: qubits and couplers are superconducting loops broken by Josephson junctions; without reliable junctions there is no annealer.
the chip must stay at millikelvin temperatures to remain superconducting and resist thermal noise.
setting and reading thousands of flux biases requires precise, low-noise electronics.
chip graphs are not fully connected, so problems must be mapped onto them — often with large overhead that limits practical problem size.

prerequisites.tech: Error correction or error mitigation for annealing
prerequisites.why: current devices can be trapped by noise or settle in excited states; no scalable error-correction scheme has been demonstrated for annealing.

pathway.milestone: commercial annealers with thousands of qubits (for example D-Wave's Advantage systems) used in hybrid quantum-classical workflows
pathway.unlocks: hands-on exploration of scheduling, portfolio and materials-search problems, though clear quantum speedup is still unproven.

pathway.milestone: higher-connectivity topologies (such as D-Wave's Zephyr design) and longer coherence
pathway.unlocks: less embedding overhead, so larger and more natural problems can be represented directly.

pathway.milestone: integrated error mitigation or logical qubits in annealing hardware
pathway.unlocks: answers that are reliable enough to trust on hard, real-world instances.

pathway.milestone: demonstrated quantum advantage on a commercially relevant optimisation task
pathway.unlocks: adoption in logistics, finance, energy and materials discovery, and a clearer role alongside gate-based quantum computers.
